parts.title: Reading Feelings More Accurately: Improving Senti-BERT and BiLSTM-Attention to Tell Positive and Negative Sentiment
parts.abstract:
Abstract

When people post on social media, they often mix words, emojis and pictures, and the meaning can be tricky to pin down. We wanted to solve the problem that computers are not accurate enough at sorting such posts into positive or negative feelings. We built a new method that combines two existing tools. The first is Senti-BERT, a type of AI model called a Transformer that reads a whole piece of text at once. The second is BiLSTM-Attention, a model that reads a text word by word, from both the start and the end, and learns which parts matter most.

Our method works in three steps. First, we add a list of known feeling words, called an emotion dictionary, to guide Senti-BERT as it turns each word into a number. We also give the model a way to decide, case by case, how much weight to give to text, emojis and pictures. Second, we use the layered attention design of BiLSTM-Attention to help the model understand the context around each word. Finally, we use a method called stacking to combine the strengths of several models.

Our experiments show that the method performs well in many ways. To judge how well it picks out feeling words, we used a score called the F1 score, which combines how many of the real feeling words it finds with how many of the words it flags really are feeling words. Our method reached an F1 score of 84.6% for feeling words that are verbs and 90.1% for feeling words that are adjectives. That is 4.8% higher than the original Transformer model. When we combined all three kinds of input (text, emojis and pictures), the model sorted posts correctly 89.4% of the time. In tests on English, its accuracy was above 90%. With our changing-weight attention, the model correctly found the exact part of a post that carried the feeling 90% of the time. We also shrank the model so it runs faster, a step called quantization. Even with 10,000 requests arriving at the same time, it still took only 92 milliseconds to answer. Stacking raised a measure called AUC, which shows how well a model tells apart positive and negative posts, to 0.943. By designing a new system with several layers, we offer a highly accurate way to study feelings on social media.
parts.introduction_first:
Social media has grown very fast, and the posts people write have grown enormously. Those posts carry a lot of information about how people feel, which is useful for keeping track of public opinion, studying markets and building smart services. Sentiment analysis is a key task in natural language processing, the field of teaching computers to understand human language. It means a computer automatically working out whether a piece of writing leans positive or negative. This helps us understand how people behave and how society changes [1].

As the amount of data has grown larger and more complicated, older methods have run into limits. They are not very good at turning words into useful information, and they do not carry over well to new situations [2]. The earliest methods relied on lists of feeling words and on fixed rules. People could easily see how these methods reached their answers, but the methods struggled to keep up as language changed [3]. Later, machine learning methods learned from examples instead of following fixed rules, so they worked better on new data. Even so, people still had to choose for them by hand which features to look at, and this made it hard to capture the full, complicated meaning of a text.

In recent years, deep learning, a kind of machine learning built from many layers of connected units, has greatly improved sentiment analysis. These models learn the whole job from start to finish, from the raw text to the final answer. In particular, models that read text word by word, called recurrent neural networks, and models that learn which parts of a text matter most, called attention mechanisms, are very good at understanding context [4]. Pre-trained language models have also helped. These models first learn from huge amounts of text, and then they can be reused for new tasks. They understand meaning better, work well in many languages and in languages with little data, and they have opened up a new way of doing sentiment analysis [5].

Despite this progress, today's methods still struggle with complicated texts and with posts that mix different kinds of input. On one hand, current models have trouble linking words that are far apart in a text and picking up subtle feelings, so they cannot fully capture the hidden meaning of a context. On the other hand, most studies look at text alone and do not combine other kinds of input, such as emojis and pictures, in a useful way. This limits how well they can capture the many different ways people express feelings [6,7]. On top of that, models are not clearly guided to find the words that carry sentiment and opinion, which holds back their performance even further.

To tackle these problems, we propose an improved way of sorting posts by sentiment. It combines an improved Senti-BERT with a BiLSTM-Attention design. We add a mechanism guided by a list of feeling words to help the model understand meaning. We use the BiLSTM-Attention design to better understand context and to pick out the key feeling words. We also process text, emojis and pictures together, so the model can combine the feelings they each carry. Finally, we combine several models, which makes the whole system work better on new data and more dependable, so it sorts sentiment more accurately in complicated situations.
parts.conclusion:
6. Conclusion

In this study, we put forward a new way of improving how computers sort posts by feeling. It combines Senti-BERT with BiLSTM-Attention, and our experiments show that it breaks through in three main areas. For accuracy, the F1 score reaches 84.6% for feeling words that are verbs and 90.1% for feeling words that are adjectives, and combining all kinds of input gives an accuracy of 89.4%. For working across languages, the model sorts English posts correctly more than 90% of the time, and it reaches 60% on zero-shot transfer learning, which means it can handle a new language without being trained on it. For real-world performance, the shrunken (quantized) model takes 92 milliseconds to answer even when 10,000 requests arrive at the same time, and stacking raises the AUC score to 0.943.

Our results offer a highly accurate way to study feelings on social media. The key new ideas are these. A mechanism guided by an emotion dictionary helps the model adapt to different kinds of writing. Layered attention lets the model pinpoint exactly where the feeling lies in a post. And a changing-weight way of combining text, emojis and pictures makes the model use each kind of input more efficiently. These advances move forward the theory of affective computing, the study of how computers can understand and respond to human feelings. They also give reliable technical support for real uses such as keeping track of public opinion and helping people communicate across cultures. In future work, we will focus on improving models that mix different approaches to sentiment, and on helping the model work better in languages with little data, so that these methods can be used in even more situations.
parts.methods:
3. Methods and materials

3.1 Improving Senti-BERT to pick up feelings better

Social media has grown very fast, and Weibo has become an important place for keeping track of and studying public opinion. Its huge number of users keep sharing updates and opinions as they happen. These posts come in several kinds of input: text, pictures and emojis. Together they tell us a lot about how people feel.

Even so, today's methods for studying feelings still have big limits. Older approaches lean too heavily on the words alone. They overlook how much pictures and emojis add to the way people express feelings, so they do not fully understand complicated meanings or the subtle details of a situation. On top of that, most existing tools only decide whether a post is positive, negative or neutral. They do not dig deeper to find what actually triggered the feeling, or why. This makes their results much less useful in practice and harder to explain.

To fix these problems, we propose a new model that combines Senti-BERT with BiLSTM-Attention to study feelings. It brings together three parts. The first is Senti-BERT, which understands the deep meaning of words. The second is BiLSTM-Attention, which reads a text word by word from both ends and learns which parts matter most. The third is a way of blending meaning from several levels. Together, these parts let the model capture how words and pictures work together to express a feeling. The model works from start to finish, from the raw text to the final answer, as shown in Fig 1.

This design does more than correctly spot whether a user's feeling leans positive or negative. It also digs into the topics that set off the feeling and the way the words are put together. In this way, it moves from the surface of a feeling down to the deeper reasons behind it. That gives more scientific and complete technical support for keeping track of public opinion, studying how users feel about a product or service, and helping society manage people's feelings.

Fig 1

Diagram of the BERT-BiLSTM model.

As Fig 1 shows, our model has four main parts: a data preparation part, a Senti-BERT part that pulls out features, a BiLSTM-Attention part that builds up context, and a part that sorts posts by feeling.

First, the data preparation part cleans up the raw text. It uses regular expressions, which are patterns that find and remove unwanted bits such as HTML tags and web addresses. It then splits the Chinese text into words and removes stop words, which are common words like "the" or "and" that carry little meaning. This makes the data cleaner and gives the next steps a standard input [21,22].

Next, the Senti-BERT part turns the cleaned text into numbers, called vectors, using a pre-trained language model. We also add a mechanism guided by a list of feeling words. It strengthens how the model handles feeling words and opinion words, so the emotional meaning stands out more. This mechanism keeps a changing balance between the meaning of the words and the feeling they carry, which makes the model better at recognizing sentiment [23,24].

After that, the BiLSTM-Attention part looks at the order of the words. A bidirectional long short-term memory network (BiLSTM) reads the text from both the start and the end, so it can see how each word relates to the words before and after it. An attention mechanism then gives different weights to the features at different points in the text. This brings out the key emotional information and produces a richer description of the context that makes it easier to tell feelings apart [25].

Finally, the sorting part takes the combined features and passes them to a Softmax classifier. This is a standard tool that turns a set of scores into chances for each category, here the sentiment categories. Because the model pulls out and blends features at several levels, it can go all the way from raw text to sentiment labels.

We also turned emojis and pictures into vectors, as shown in equation (1). Equation (1) follows the usual way of turning these inputs into numbers: a pre-trained language model for text, a convolutional neural network (CNN) for pictures, and a residual visual encoding method for emojis. A CNN is a type of model that is very good at spotting patterns in images. We adapted this general approach so that text, emojis and pictures all end up as the same kind of vector [26].

(1) m = f_BERT(M),  e = f_CNN(E),  v = f_ResNet(I)

In equation (1), m stands for the text features, e for the emoji features and v for the picture features. f_BERT is the part that turns text into numbers, and M is the input text. f_CNN is the part that turns emojis into numbers, and E is the emoji image. f_ResNet is the part that turns pictures into numbers, and I is the input picture.

Building on these vectors, we then worked out in more detail how to pull out and blend the picture features. First, we resized all the input pictures to the same size. Then we used a pre-trained CNN to pull out high-level features, meaning the deeper meaning behind what is shown. We turned these picture features into the same kind of numbers as the text features, using a simple straight-line calculation called a linear mapping. This lets the two kinds of input line up with each other.

We did not simply join the picture and emoji features onto the end. Instead, we fed them in after Senti-BERT had turned the text into its vectors, but before the deep processing stage. That way, they take part in the later work on meaning and help the model describe the feeling in context. The lined-up picture and emoji features are combined with the text vectors at an in-between layer. So they are adjusted together with the context processing, rather than treated as separate inputs.

To decide how much each kind of input counts, we used a changing-weight strategy. During training, the model adjusts how much each kind of input contributes, depending on how important it is in each particular post. In other words, the model learns to give text, pictures and emojis different importance as it picks up how relevant each one is in each case. It does this through a learnable structure that works a bit like a gate, which lets the model turn up the useful inputs and turn down the less relevant ones. As a result, picture features can be boosted when they match the meaning of the text, or faded when they add noise or confusion. This avoids the problems of fixed weights and makes combining the inputs more effective and more dependable.

The picture features are then blended with the text features to give the text a richer description of its feelings, so the model can capture emotional information more fully. The calculation is shown in equation (2). This way of blending follows a common approach that gives each kind of input a weight. Unlike simply joining inputs with fixed weights, the weights in our study are learnable, which means the model adjusts how much text, emoji and picture features count as it trains [27].

(2) h = α_t + β_e + γ_v

In equation (2), h stands for the blended emotional features from all the inputs. α, β and γ are the learnable weights. These weights are not set by hand but are learned automatically during training. You can think of this as a way of choosing which features to focus on, guided by attention. It lowers the risk of overfitting, which happens when a model memorizes its training examples instead of learning general patterns. The learned weights also stay fairly steady across different training runs and different ways of splitting the data, which shows that the method copes well with changes in the weights.

After blending the inputs in equation (2), we train the whole model from start to finish using a combined loss function. A loss function is a score of how wrong the model's answers are, and training means adjusting the model to make this score smaller. The total loss function, L_total, is defined in equation (3). We designed it following a common deep learning idea of aiming for several goals at once. The sorting loss is the main goal. The dictionary-guided loss and the regularization loss are extra helpers. The dictionary-guided loss uses the list of feeling words to strengthen the model's description of sentiment. The regularization loss keeps the model from becoming too complicated, which helps prevent overfitting [28].

(3) L_total = ε L_cls + μ L_lex + λ L_reg

In equation (3), L_cls is the sorting loss, L_lex is the dictionary-guided loss and L_reg is the regularization loss. ε is the weight for the main task and is set to 0.7. μ is the weight for the dictionary task and is set to 0.2. λ is the regularization setting and is set to 0.1.

3.2 Improving the BiLSTM-Attention design

In sentiment analysis, the Senti-BERT layer is good at picking out small, local emotional features, because it combines an emotion dictionary with a way of blending the different kinds of input. However, traditional Transformer models have trouble with feelings that are spread far apart in a text. This is a problem when a post stretches over a long time or has a complicated context, which is common in social media. Ordinary LSTM models struggle to capture deep links between emotional signals. Basic attention mechanisms often fail to focus precisely on the key emotional parts, so the model's overall picture of the feeling ends up incomplete and inconsistent.

To solve these problems, we propose an improved BiLSTM-Attention design with several layers. It uses BiLSTM to capture long-range features, meaning links between words far apart in the text, and the context around them. It also adds a layered way of sharing out attention weights, which improves the model in three ways. First, it builds a consistent picture of emotional clues that cross from one sentence to the next, so scattered feelings are joined together. Second, it improves how the model works out the relationships between feeling words, so it can better work out hidden emotional logic. Third, it lets text and other kinds of input, such as pictures and emojis, blend and respond to each other as the model goes. This design greatly improves the model's ability to understand the overall meaning of a feeling, and it offers an effective way to understand feelings deeply in complicated social media settings. Fig 2 shows the design in detail.

Fig 2

Diagram of the BiLSTM model.

Fig 2 shows the layered design of BiLSTM. Its input features come from the output sequence (x1, x2, x3, x4, ..., xn) of the Senti-BERT layer. The design builds up context using two processing units that run side by side. A forward LSTM reads the text in order and picks up the context from earlier words. A backward LSTM reads it in reverse and picks up the context from later words. Finally, the two are joined into one combined vector by putting their features end to end, as shown in equation (4). This two-way reading follows the standard way BiLSTM represents a sequence. In our study, the forward and backward results are then blended using a changing weight, which strengthens the description of the feeling in context [29].

(4) F→ = LSTM_f(h1(f), h2(f), ..., h_T(f)),  B← = LSTM_b(h1(b), h2(b), ..., h_N(b)),  H = ωF→ + (1 − ω)B←

In equation (4), F→ is the final result of the forward LSTM, and LSTM_f is the LSTM unit that reads forward. h_k(f) is the hidden state of the forward pass at step k. A hidden state is the running summary a model keeps as it reads along. B← is the final result of the backward LSTM, and LSTM_b is the LSTM unit that reads backward. h_m(b) is the hidden state at step m of the backward pass. H is the combined features after blending. ω is the changing weight, which can take any value from 0 to 1.

When we studied the Sina Weibo data closely, we found that existing methods for studying feelings are clearly weak at handling emojis. Traditional models often treat emojis as fixed labels for feelings and ignore how their meaning changes from one context to another. To capture how emojis relate to each other, we built an emoji relationship network based on which common emojis appear together in the data. First, we counted how often each pair of emojis appears in the same text. Then we used the context descriptions of the emojis to calculate a cosine similarity, a measure of how closely two things are related, as a sign of how strongly they are linked in meaning. Next, we treated each emoji as a point, or node, and each similarity value as the weight of the line, or edge, between two nodes. This gave us a network, shown in Fig 3.

Fig 3

Network of emoji symbols.

In Fig 3, 12 common emojis are used in many different kinds of text and express feelings in clearly different ways. A single label for each emoji's feeling cannot capture its true meaning accurately. To get around this, we propose a new plan in three stages.

First, we build an emoji network from a large amount of Weibo data and measure how closely the emojis are linked in meaning using statistical methods. In this network, the weight of each node shows how often that emoji is used, and the weight of each edge shows how likely two emojis are to appear together. This is written as equation (5). The similarity measure in equation (5) comes from counting how often emojis appear together, and it is related in idea to cosine similarity. We adapted it to judge how strongly two emojis are linked in meaning by comparing how often they appear together with how often each one appears on its own [30].

(5) sim(e_i, e_j) = freq(e_i ∩ e_j) / (freq(e_i) × freq(e_j))

In equation (5), sim(e_i, e_j) is the similarity between emojis e_i and e_j. freq(e_i ∩ e_j) is how often e_i and e_j appear together in the data. freq(e_i) is how often e_i appears on its own, and freq(e_j) is how often e_j appears on its own. The measure in equation (5) comes from counting how often emojis appear together and is related in idea to cosine similarity. It divides how often a pair of emojis appears together by how often each one appears on its own, which gives a more balanced picture of how they are linked in meaning.

Second, we design a layered attention system that adjusts itself, to deal with the fact that traditional attention mechanisms do not handle emojis well enough. This system works out the weight of each emoji as it goes, by using the two-way LSTM to pick up the context. Our layered attention does not follow the usual pattern of one level for words and one level for sentences. Instead, it has two levels. One gives attention to each time step in the BiLSTM output. The other blends the text, emoji and picture features. Together they describe sentiment at several levels. The calculation is shown in equation (6). This way of calculating attention weights follows the general attention mechanism used in neural networks. In our study, the attention score at each time step takes into account both the BiLSTM hidden state and the emoji feature. This lets key emotional parts, and emojis whose meaning depends on the context, get higher weights [31].

(6) θ_t = exp(W^T [h_t; e_t]) / Σ_{k=1}^{T} exp(W^T [h_k; e_k])

In equation (6), θ_t is the attention weight at time t. W^T is a weight matrix, a table of numbers that the model learns. h_t is the hidden state of the LSTM at time t, and e_t is the emoji feature at time t. T is the total number of time steps in the sequence, and k is a temporary counter used in the calculation.

BiLSTM layers cannot tell apart how important different words are for sentiment analysis. So we added attention mechanisms to give each word a weight based on its meaning, which makes the sorting more accurate. When we combine BiLSTM with attention, we replace the original softmax layer with an attention layer. The softmax function then turns the scores into chances. In the stage where meaning is combined, self-attention layers weight and add the text and emoji features to calculate scores for each category. Then a straight-line calculation, called a linear transformation, turns the features into the final form used for sentiment analysis. This is shown in equation (7). The nonlinear transformation in equation (7) follows the standard way neural networks map features. It uses learned weight matrices and a nonlinear activation function, a mathematical step that bends the numbers, to project different inputs into a shared hidden space. This helps the different kinds of meaning interact with each other [32].

(7) D = tanh(W_s · S + W_r · R + b)

In equation (7), W_s and W_r are weight matrices, S and R are the two input vectors, and b is a bias vector, a set of extra numbers added to the result. In the sentiment analysis stage, we use the softmax function to sort the text by feeling. Feelings are strictly split into two categories: positive and negative. The exact calculation and the loss function L are shown in equation (8). The softmax function and the cross-entropy loss in equation (8) are standard tools for sorting posts by feeling with neural networks. The softmax function turns sentiment scores into chances for each category. The cross-entropy loss measures how far the predicted chances are from the correct answers, and the model adjusts its settings to make this loss smaller, based on the true labels [33].

(8) p_c = exp(d_c) / Σ_{r=1}^{c} exp(d_r),  L = Σ_{d∈D} Σ_{c=1}^{c} p_{c_g(d)}(log p_c(d))

In equation (8), p_c is the predicted chance of category c, and d_c is the original score for category c. d_r is the original score for category r, and r is the index of the categories. c is the total number of categories. d is the input data, and D is the training dataset. p_{c_g(d)} is the true label of sample d, and p_c(d) is the predicted chance for sample d.

3.3 Improving the way we combine several models

We have already done the early steps: collecting the data, cleaning it, labeling it and turning the different kinds of input into vectors. Even so, sentiment analysis still faces serious challenges. The models do not carry over well to new data, and they look at only a limited number of features. These problems greatly limit how accurate and explainable the models are in real, complicated situations, and they hold back how deeply we can dig into the meaning of feelings. A single model often struggles to capture the many different, hidden emotional patterns in social media posts. Its performance drops sharply when it is moved to a new kind of data, when the writing style changes, or when it crosses cultures.

To tackle these limits, we propose a way of combining several models. It brings together the strengths of models with different designs, so the whole system is better at telling feelings apart and more stable. The main job of combining models is to bring together the predictions of several base models, the models that do the actual work. This can be done in ways such as weighted voting, stacking or meta-learning, where a final model learns from the predictions of the others. Combining models in this way reduces the possible biases and the risk of overfitting that come with a single model, which makes the predictions more accurate and more dependable. It also helps the system adapt to unknown data and to data from other kinds of writing. Because it uses features and decision-making from several viewpoints and at several levels, it keeps performing well even when the new data differs from the training data, and it carries over better to new situations. To help the models work together efficiently and fill in each other's gaps, we built a well-organized system for combining them, shown in Fig 4.

Fig 4

Diagram of how the models are combined.

Fig 4 shows that the dataset is split into a training set, used to learn, and a validation set, used to check the results. Three pre-trained models turn the data into text vectors. These vectors go into the BiLSTM model, which gives the sentiment results. This shows that combining models makes sentiment analysis more accurate. The diagrams guide how the models are combined, which helps them learn and analyze features efficiently.

We chose stacking to combine the BERT model, because it brings together the predictions of the base models through layered training, which improves performance and reduces overfitting. Other ways of combining models have drawbacks. Bagging, which trains several models on random samples of the data and averages their answers, makes results more stable but improves predictions only a little. Boosting, which trains models one after another with each correcting the last, gradually improves performance but can lead to overfitting and makes training complicated. Blending, which averages the models' outputs, may not work as well as stacking when the data is unbalanced or the task is complicated. Combining BERT models needs to bring together their full strengths and balance stability with performance, and stacking is the best choice because it trains in layers and brings the results together. Fig 5 shows the steps of stacking.

Fig 5

Flow chart of the stacking method.

Fig 5 shows how stacking works in layers. Several sets of base models, the models that do the actual work, process the raw data side by side and each give their own predictions. These in-between results become new inputs for a meta model, a final model that learns a second time from them. The final output is the combined prediction. In our study, we use logistic regression as the meta model to blend the outputs of the base models with weights. Logistic regression is a simple model that learns how likely each category is.

We chose logistic regression because the base models, such as Senti-BERT and BiLSTM-Attention, already give predictions as chances of each category. So the main job of the stacking stage is to adjust and combine these outputs, not to add more complicated transformations. Logistic regression works directly with chances, so the results keep the same meaning as probabilities, and it can combine the outputs of different models well. Also, the meta model in stacking usually has only a small amount of data to learn from. A simple linear model with few parts helps lower the risk of overfitting and makes the results more stable on new data. Compared with simple averaging or voting, logistic regression learns how much each base model should count based on how reliable its predictions are, which gives a more principled and flexible way of combining them. And compared with more complicated meta models such as neural networks, it strikes a good balance between how complicated the model is and how well it combines the others. This design brings together the variety of the base models and the higher-level combination of their features, through two levels of modeling.

In summary, we propose a way of improving how feelings are sorted that combines an improved Senti-BERT with BiLSTM-Attention. The method first turns the text into vectors with the Senti-BERT layer. Then the BiLSTM-Attention model picks out the context features, and the attention mechanisms strengthen the recognition of key emotional features. We also add a way of combining several models, especially stacking, to make the model carry over better to new data and predict more accurately. By blending several levels and several kinds of input in this way, the model can understand and analyze emotional information in complicated texts more effectively, which offers a new solution for sorting posts by feeling.
parts.results:
4. Results

4.1 Checking how well the main parts of our model work

We ran a series of experiments to test how well our combined model, Senti-BERT joined with BiLSTM-Attention, sorts posts by feeling. We judged it from several angles: how accurate it is, how quickly it works, and how well it adapts to different situations. We also looked at the data itself. About 35% of the posts were positive, 33% were negative and 32% were neutral, so the three groups were fairly evenly balanced.

To make sure our results were reliable and that others could repeat them, we set up a careful, fixed system for the experiments, shown in Table 1. It covers the whole chain, from the computer hardware to the code. We paid special attention to keeping the working conditions, the data quality and the training steps the same every time. Our design also took into account that real posts mix text, emojis and pictures, and that the model will be used in industry. We then checked the model's performance with numbers and by comparing it with other models.

Table 1

Basic settings for our experiments.

| Setting | Item | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Hardware | GPU (graphics card) | NVIDIA V100/ A100/ T4 |
| | Memory | 32 GB DDR4 |
| | Storage | NVMe SSD (1 TB) |
| Software | Python | 3.8+ |
| | Framework | PyTorch 1.12.0 |
| | CUDA/cuDNN | CUDA 11.7/ cuDNN 8.5 |
| Model | Senti-BERT | 12 layers, 768 hidden size, 12 heads |
| | BiLSTM | 2 layers, 512 units |
| | Attention | Changing-weight attention (64-dim) |
| Training | Optimizer (learning method) | AdamW (5e-5) |
| | Batch size | 32 |
| | Epochs (full passes through the data) | 50 |
| | Loss (error measure) | Combined loss (main task weight 0.7) |
| Data | Dataset | 50,000 Weibo samples |
| | Split | 8:1:1 |
| | Text length | 512 |
| | Image size | 224 × 224 |
| Reproducibility | Random seed | 42 |
| | Initialization | Xavier |
| | Early stopping | 5 epochs |

To see how much Senti-BERT helps with picking out feeling words, we compared it with four other models: the original BERT, RoBERTa (a more robust version of BERT), ELECTRA and Senti-BERT. We judged them mainly by the F1 score. We also looked at how many of the real feeling words each model found, and at a confusion matrix, a table that shows which answers a model mixes up with which. Fig 6 shows the results.

Fig 6

How well each pre-trained language model picks out feelings, judged in several ways.

Fig 6(a) shows that Senti-BERT was best at picking out feeling words that are verbs, with an F1 score of 84.6 ± 0.6. The "± 0.6" shows how much the score varied across repeated runs. That is 4.8% higher than the original BERT, and Senti-BERT reached 90.1% for feeling words that are adjectives.

Fig 6(b) shows that Senti-BERT found the most real feeling words, at 85.2%. It took a little longer to answer, 46.9 milliseconds, than ELECTRA. Its confusion matrix also had the lowest entropy, 0.152. Entropy here measures how mixed-up the model's mistakes are, so a lower value means fewer kinds of mix-ups.

These results show that Senti-BERT did outstandingly on tasks with complicated meaning, thanks to its improved emotion dictionary. Still, it could work faster. This confirms that its design, which combines several kinds of input, strikes a balance between accuracy and speed.

Next, we wanted to check whether BiLSTM-Attention is better at following how a feeling builds up over a long text. We compared it with a standard LSTM, a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU, a simpler version of LSTM), a Transformer and BiLSTM-Attention. We mainly looked at how well each model linked feelings that are far apart in a text. We also checked how consistent it was with the surrounding context, and how accurately it found the key feeling parts. Fig 7 shows the results.

Fig 7

How well each pre-trained language model performs, judged in several ways.

Fig 7(a) shows that BiLSTM-Attention did best on how well it understood meaning. Its accuracy and consistency scores were clearly higher than those of the Transformer, which came second: 1.7% higher in accuracy and 0.05% higher in consistency.

Fig 7(b) shows that BiLSTM-Attention was also fast. It found the key feeling parts correctly 78.6% of the time, which is 5% to 8% better than the models we compared it with. It took 53.8 milliseconds to answer, only 11.7 milliseconds slower than the fastest model, the GRU.

By combining several kinds of input and keeping its design light, BiLSTM-Attention reached the best balance between accuracy and speed. It clearly did better on complicated meaning, which confirms that our new design works.

To check whether combining text, emojis and pictures really helps, we ran ablation experiments. In these, we take parts of the model away one at a time to see what each part adds. We compared models that used only one kind of input with models that combined several. The models that combined several used our weighted way of combining inputs and our way of turning each kind of input into numbers. We judged them by how well the feelings from different inputs agreed, how well the inputs filled in for each other, and how accurately the model sorted posts. Table 2 shows the results.

Table 2

Results for models using one or several kinds of input.

| Input used | Agreement between inputs | Sorting accuracy | F1 score for irony | How well inputs fill in for each other | Time to answer (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Text only | 0.72 ± 0.03 | 83.1 ± 0.5 | 65.2 ± 1.2 | / | 42.1 |
| Emojis only | 0.68 ± 0.04 | 71.3 ± 0.8 | 58.7 ± 1.5 | / | 18.6 |
| Picture only | 0.65 ± 0.05 | 69.8 ± 0.9 | 52.4 ± 1.8 | / | 23.4 |
| Text + Emojis | 0.81 ± 0.02 | 86.7 ± 0.4 | 73.5 ± 1.0 | 0.63 | 47.3 |
| Text + Picture | 0.79 ± 0.02 | 85.9 ± 0.4 | 70.8 ± 1.1 | 0.58 | 51.2 |
| All inputs combined | 0.89 ± 0.01 | 89.4 ± 0.3 | 78.6 ± 0.8 | 0.72 | 53.8 |

As Table 2 shows, the model that combined all inputs led in every way. Its agreement between inputs was 0.89, its sorting accuracy was 89.4%, and its F1 score for irony was 78.6%. All of these were clearly better than the other setups. Compared with the text-only model, they were 17%, 6.3% and 13.4% higher.

When we used two kinds of input, text with emojis did better than text with pictures, both at spotting irony and at speed. This confirms that emojis help with complicated meaning. Models that used only one kind of input did worst, and the picture-only model had the lowest scores of all. This shows how much it matters to combine several kinds of input. Combining all of them gave the best balance between accuracy and speed, because each kind of input filled in for the others, especially for tricky meaning such as irony.

We also wanted to know whether the weights we give to the emotion dictionary matter a lot. So we ran a sensitivity analysis, which tests how much the results change when we change one setting. We multiplied the weight of the dictionary terms by different amounts, within a small range, and kept everything else the same. Table 3 shows the results.

Table 3

How changing the weight of the emotion dictionary affects the model.

| Dictionary weight | Accuracy (%) | F1 score (%) |
|---|---|---|
| 0.8× | 88.91 | 88.25 |
| 0.9× | 89.18 | 88.52 |
| 1.0× | 89.40 | 88.76 |
| 1.1× | 89.27 | 88.61 |
| 1.2× | 89.05 | 88.33 |

Table 3 shows that the model's performance stays steady when the dictionary weights change a little. Accuracy moved by no more than 0.5%. This means our way of setting the weights does not depend too closely on exact values, and it does not need to be tuned for each new dataset. The effect of the dictionary is therefore well controlled, and the model is robust and works well on new data.

To check how well our changing-weight attention works for sentiment analysis, we compared it with two simpler kinds of attention. Average attention gives every word the same weight. Self-attention gives each word a weight based only on the other words in the same text. Our model uses layered changing-weight attention. We compared the three on how accurately they picked out feeling words, their F1 score for sorting feelings, how evenly their weights were spread (measured with a value called KL divergence), how long they took to train, their F1 score for whole paragraphs, and how easy it was to see how they worked. Fig 8 shows the results.

Fig 8

How different kinds of attention compare, judged in several ways.

Fig 8(a) shows that changing-weight attention picked out key parts correctly about 90% of the time and reached an F1 score of 0.85 for whole paragraphs. Both were clearly better than self-attention and average attention. It did take a little longer to train, which shows the trade-off between accuracy and computing cost. Self-attention was fairly balanced between speed and performance, while average attention came last overall.

Fig 8(b) shows that changing-weight attention scored 4.7 on how easy it was to understand, with a KL divergence of 0.12. This means its weights matched the pattern of feelings in the data best. Self-attention came second, and average attention did worst, because it gave every word the same weight.

These results show that changing-weight attention was best for accuracy, for handling long texts and for being easy to understand, so it suits demanding tasks. Self-attention balanced speed and performance, making it a good but not the best choice. Average attention was only suitable for simple cases, which confirms that layered changing weights are better.

To check whether stacking really improves how several models combine their inputs, we compared it with three other ways of combining models: Bagging, Boosting and Blending. Bagging trains several models separately and averages their answers. Boosting trains models one after another, with each new one fixing the mistakes of the last. Blending trains models separately and then blends their answers. As the base models, we used BERT, a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN, a model that is good at pictures) and Random Forest (RF, a method that combines many simple decision trees). We judged them by accuracy, AUC and other measures. Fig 9 shows the results.

Fig 9

How stacking compares with other ways of combining models, using different base models.

Fig 9(a) and 9(b) show that as the dataset became more complicated, the accuracy of every method went up. Stacking reached the highest accuracy, 88%, when it combined BERT, CNN and RF, which is 2% higher than the best single base model. The AUC scores in Fig 9(c) and 9(d) followed a similar pattern. Stacking reached a peak AUC of 96% with the combined model, clearly better than Boosting's 94% and Blending's 92%. Bagging did poorly on small datasets but improved a lot as the data grew.

Adding the extra models raised the performance of each method by 1% to 3%. Stacking always did best, especially on complicated data, which shows how combining several models strengthens models that handle several kinds of input.

4.2 How well the model works across many situations and languages

To check whether transfer learning helps when there is little data, we ran an experiment on how efficiently models learn from small amounts of data. Transfer learning means reusing a model that has already learned from a lot of other data. We took between 1% and 100% of the data, in steps, and compared pre-trained models such as BERT and ResNet-50 (a 50-layer image model) with traditional methods such as Support Vector Machine (SVM) and RF. We looked at how steeply each model's learning curve rose, its accuracy on the test data, and its F1 score at different amounts of data. We kept the random seeds for choosing the data and the model settings the same, so the comparison was fair. Fig 10 shows the results.

Fig 10

How different models perform with different amounts of data.

Fig 10(a) compares how efficiently the models learn. The steepness of the learning curve shows how much accuracy a model gains for each extra bit of data. At 80% of the data, ResNet-50 had a steepness of 0.85 and BERT 0.82, while SVM and RF reached only 0.68 and 0.72.

Fig 10(b) shows how accuracy changed as more data was added. ResNet-50 reached the highest accuracy, 92%, on the full dataset. On just 20% of the data, BERT still reached 78%, beating SVM's 65% and RF's 70%. As the amount of data grew, every model's accuracy rose steadily.

Fig 10(c) brings all of this together. With 50% of the data, BERT reached an F1 score of 88.64%, better than RF's 82.39% and SVM's 79.68%. ResNet-50 stayed in the lead, with an F1 score above 90% at 80% of the data.

These results show that deep learning models kept their advantage more steadily across different amounts of data. Traditional models closed the gap a lot once there was enough data.

To check how well the BERT-BiLSTM model handles posts with mixed feelings, we built a made-up dataset containing both positive and negative feelings. We compared BERT-BiLSTM with three other methods: L-MLkNN, BERT+Softmax and AMLL. We judged them by how many mixed feelings they found, their Hamming loss (the share of labels they got wrong), their AUC score and how long they took to train. Fig 11 shows the results.

Fig 11

How models compare on posts with mixed feelings, judged in several ways.

Fig 11(a) shows that BERT-BiLSTM+Softmax found mixed feelings 80% of the time (a recall of 0.8) and had a Hamming loss of 0.1, which was clearly better than L-MLkNN and AMLL.

Fig 11(b) shows that BERT-BiLSTM had the highest AUC score, 0.9, but it took nearly 60 seconds to train. L-MLkNN trained fastest, in only 40 seconds, but it had the lowest AUC score, just 0.6. AMLL was balanced in between.

These results show that BERT-BiLSTM+Softmax led in accuracy and suits demanding situations.

To check whether BERT-BiLSTM works in languages other than Chinese, we tested it on English, Indonesian and Hebrew. We prepared the data in the same way for every language, turning text, emojis and pictures into numbers. We compared BERT-BiLSTM with two other methods: XLM-R (Cross-lingual Language Model Robust) and mBERT (Multi-lingual BERT). We judged them by how much their accuracy varied between languages, by their macro-average F1 score (the average of the F1 scores for each language), and by their zero-shot transfer accuracy, meaning how well they handled a new language without being trained on it. To keep the comparison fair, every model used the same number of dimensions and the same number of training passes. Fig 12 shows the final results.

Fig 12

How models compare across languages, and how well transfer learning works.

Fig 12(a) compares how accurately four models sorted posts in English, Indonesian and Hebrew. BERT-BiLSTM had the highest accuracy in all three languages: above 90% in English, above 85% in Indonesian and above 80% in Hebrew. This shows it stays steady across languages.

Fig 12(b) shows that BERT-BiLSTM had the highest zero-shot transfer value, about 85%, and the lowest variance, meaning its results changed the least from run to run. This shows it was the best at transfer learning.

These results show that BERT-BiLSTM did best both at sorting posts in several languages and at handling new languages without training, balancing accuracy with working on new data. The other models did much worse when the language changed.

To see how fast our model works in real industry settings, where many requests arrive at the same time, we ran tests on a group of NVIDIA T4 graphics cards. We simulated between 1,000 and 10,000 requests per second (QPS). We compared three models: Senti-BERT alone, BiLSTM-Attention alone, and our combined model (Senti-BERT + BiLSTM). We also compared them with a lightweight model, MobileNetV3, a small model designed for speed. Every model was tested with the same amount of data and the same input setup, so the comparison was fair. Table 4 shows the results.

Table 4

How models perform with different numbers of requests arriving at the same time.

| Requests per second | Model | Time to answer (ms) | P99 time (ms) | Memory (GB) | Throughput (requests per second) | Accuracy (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1000 | Senti-BERT | 31 | 40 | 4.0 | 960 | 87.1 |
| | BiLSTM-Attention | 35 | 46 | 3.6 | 940 | 86.5 |
| | Senti-BERT + BiLSTM (combined) | 28 | 35 | 4.2 | 980 | 88.7 |
| | MobileNetV3 | 21 | 29 | 2.1 | 950 | 82.4 |
| 5000 | Senti-BERT | 72 | 91 | 4.3 | 4600 | 87.0 |
| | BiLSTM-Attention | 78 | 102 | 3.9 | 4450 | 86.2 |
| | Senti-BERT + BiLSTM (combined) | 63 | 79 | 4.5 | 4850 | 87.9 |
| | MobileNetV3 | 38 | 52 | 1.8 | 4620 | 80.1 |
| 10000 | Senti-BERT | 162 | 215 | 4.7 | 7600 | 86.8 |
| | Senti-BERT + BiLSTM (unshrunken) | 157 | 208 | 3.8 | 7800 | 87.2 |
| | Senti-BERT + BiLSTM (shrunken) | 92 | 121 | 3.0 | 9200 | 86.5 |

Table 4 shows that our combined model strikes a good balance between accuracy, speed and computing cost at every level of load. At 5,000 requests per second, it took 63 milliseconds to answer. That is about 12.5% faster than Senti-BERT alone, and its accuracy was about 0.9% higher. Compared with BiLSTM, its accuracy was about 1.7% higher.

At a heavy load of 10,000 requests per second, we shrank the model, and it took only 92 milliseconds to answer. It handled 9,200 requests per second, and its accuracy dropped by only 0.7%.

It is worth noting that our model combines several parts and uses stacking. Even so, compared with the single models, it took only slightly longer to answer and used only a little more memory (about 0.2 to 0.5 GB more), while it kept its performance gains and became more dependable. The lightweight model, MobileNetV3, answered faster, but its accuracy was more than 6% lower, which makes it less suitable for tasks that need high accuracy.

So our method strikes a good balance between better performance and computing cost, and it shows that it is practical and efficient for real industry use. We also use stacking mainly during training, to help the model work well on new data. When the model is in use, we shrink it and use quantization to keep the computing cost low and the cost of running it down.

To see how well our model works in new languages and new kinds of writing, we ran a transfer experiment. We used Weibo posts as the starting point and moved the model to two new kinds of data: reviews from the online shop JD, and medical texts from MIMIC-III. We ran the comparison in PyTorch on an NVIDIA V100 graphics card. We chose several well-known recent models that use different technical approaches. XLM-R (large) and mBERT were strong pre-trained models that handle many languages. A fine-tuned LLaMA-2 (7B) model, a large language model, stood for the kind of model built on very large language models. A hybrid GNN-BERT model, which adds a graph network that links related parts of a text, stood for approaches that use graphs to understand meaning. We compared all of these with our Senti-BERT + BiLSTM-Attention model. Table 5 shows the results.

Table 5

How models compare across languages and when moved to new kinds of data.

| Model | Language | Accuracy (%) | Zero-shot transfer value (%) | Variance | Macro-average F1 | Training time (hours) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Senti-BERT + BiLSTM-Attention | English | 89.3 | 66.8 | 3.2 | 0.887 | 4.5 |
| | Indonesian | 80.4 | 65.9 | 3.4 | 0.840 | 4.6 |
| | Hebrew | 77.1 | 65.1 | 3.6 | 0.818 | 4.8 |
| XLM-R (large) | English | 87.2 | 63.7 | 4.1 | 0.862 | 5.1 |
| | Indonesian | 78.6 | 62.8 | 4.3 | 0.829 | 5.3 |
| | Hebrew | 75.0 | 61.9 | 4.5 | 0.804 | 5.5 |
| mBERT | English | 84.7 | 59.3 | 4.7 | 0.842 | 4.7 |
| | Indonesian | 74.5 | 58.1 | 4.9 | 0.811 | 4.9 |
| | Hebrew | 70.8 | 57.0 | 5.1 | 0.786 | 5.0 |
| LLaMA-2 (7B, fine-tuned) | English | 90.2 | 68.5 | 5.4 | 0.894 | 12.3 |
| | Indonesian | 81.6 | 67.2 | 5.7 | 0.850 | 12.8 |
| | Hebrew | 78.3 | 66.0 | 6.0 | 0.826 | 13.2 |
| GNN-BERT (hybrid) | English | 88.4 | 65.1 | 3.8 | 0.874 | 7.2 |
| | Indonesian | 79.5 | 64.0 | 4.0 | 0.835 | 7.5 |
| | Hebrew | 76.2 | 63.3 | 4.2 | 0.812 | 7.8 |

Table 5 shows that our method performs strongly overall across languages and when moved to new kinds of data, compared with recent leading models. It beats the traditional pre-trained models, XLM-R and mBERT, on every measure: accuracy, zero-shot transfer and macro-average F1. It also has lower variance, meaning its results change less from run to run, which shows it stays steadier when moved to new kinds of data.

Compared with the hybrid GNN-BERT model, our method does slightly better or about the same, with lower variance. This suggests it can capture how words relate to each other without building a graph, so it stays both efficient and dependable. LLaMA-2 reached the highest accuracy in some cases, but it took much longer to train and varied more. Our method, by contrast, offers a better balance between performance, steadiness and computing cost.

These results show that our design still competes well with recent models built on large language models and on graphs, while being better suited to real-world use.

5. Discussion

We built on earlier research in sentiment analysis and proposed a new way of sorting posts by feeling. It combines Senti-BERT with BiLSTM-Attention, and our thorough experiments show that it works well.

Let us start with how our method fits into the history of the field. Older machine learning methods, such as those by X. Liu and colleagues [8] and F. Liu and colleagues [9], mostly relied on people choosing features by hand or on simple model designs. These methods did reasonably well on particular tasks. Even so, they still struggled to capture complicated meaning and to handle posts that mix different kinds of input. Our method is different. It adds a mechanism guided by an emotion dictionary, and it learns a deeper understanding of meaning. It reached an F1 score of 84.6% for feeling words that are verbs and 90.1% for feeling words that are adjectives. That is 4.8% higher than the original BERT model. This result shows that adding knowledge about the subject to a pre-trained model really does help it understand feelings better.

We also compared our method with recent approaches that use deep learning and pre-trained models, such as those by S. Zhang and colleagues [13] and C. Shaw and colleagues [14]. Our method improves on them in two ways. First, it combines the BiLSTM-Attention design, which helps it understand context better. Second, it uses a changing-weight way of combining text, emojis and pictures. Overall, it sorted posts correctly 89.4% of the time. These findings indirectly support the idea that each kind of input adds something the others lack, and that they work better together. They also suggest that a single, unified design can make the model's understanding of meaning more consistent.

Our method also works well across languages. It performed steadily on datasets in English, Indonesian and Hebrew. On zero-shot transfer learning, it did better than XLM-R, a pre-trained model built for many languages, and better than BERT models trained on just one language. This suggests it has strong potential to work across many languages.

Next, we look at how the models are built. Some studies, such as those by H. Jiang and colleagues [17] and T. Meng and colleagues [18], use graph neural networks. These models treat words as points in a network and learn the complicated links between them. Our method instead uses BiLSTM and attention to follow how words depend on one another in order. This lets it capture context well without building complicated networks.

We also consider how easy it is to see why a model reaches its answers. Some related work, such as that by T. M. A. U. Gunathilaka and colleagues [19] and Z. Lin and colleagues [20], makes models more transparent by picking out key sentences or by combining the answers of several "expert" models. Our method takes a different route. It uses the attention weights, which show how much the model pays attention to each part of a post, to find the key parts that carry the feeling. This gives a certain level of explainability while the model still performs strongly.

Finally, we look at how the model behaves in real use. Our model performs well when many requests arrive at the same time. The shrunken (quantized) BERT-BiLSTM model handled 9,200 requests per second, and each answer took 92 milliseconds, even when 10,000 requests arrived at the same time. Its accuracy dropped by only 0.7% compared with its normal form. This shows that our method strikes a good balance between running efficiently and staying accurate, which makes it suitable for use in real systems.

Our research still has three main limitations. First, the way the model handles the changing meaning of emojis depends on data from particular social platforms, so we still need to check how well it works on other platforms. Second, our model that mixes different approaches to sentiment could still be improved by 10% on the Hamming loss. This is a measure of how often the model gets the exact answer wrong, so a lower value is better. Third, although our model does better than the comparison models in languages with little data, its accuracy in those languages is still below 80%. These limitations match the common challenges in sentiment analysis that Bordoloi's review of the field identified. Future work will need new breakthroughs, for example through incremental pre-training, where a model keeps learning from new data over time, and through knowledge distillation, where a large model teaches a smaller one.
